title: Chapter XXXIV
summary: Jane closes the Morton school, restores Moor House, and welcomes Diana and Mary home as financially independent family. St. John increasingly directs Jane's studies, replacing German with Hindustani and discovering that her discipline can be bent to his will. Six weeks before sailing, he asks her to go to India as his wife and fellow-laborer. Jane can imagine accepting the work and even death, but not marriage without mutual love. She offers to go as his sister; he refuses because he wants a helpmeet he can influence and retain absolutely, and recasts her refusal as refusal of God.
events: The shared inheritance reunites Jane, Diana, and Mary in a restored Moor House.
St. John trains Jane in Hindustani and progressively subjects her habits to his disciplined influence.
He claims Jane as a missionary wife because her abilities suit his work.
Jane offers missionary service as a free sister but refuses a loveless marriage; St. John accepts only total marital union.

characters.name: Jane Eyre
characters.development: Now secure in money and family, recognizes that noble work cannot justify surrendering the private self through a loveless marriage.

characters.name: St. John Rivers
characters.development: Values Jane as a capable instrument of mission, identifying divine command with his own plan and demanding an absolute tie.

characters.name: Diana and Mary Rivers
characters.development: Return from governess dependence to a shared home and become a living counterweight to St. John's self-erasing vocation.

threads.text: Jane's inheritance frees the Rivers sisters and establishes Moor House as their shared home.
St. John's missionary ambition turns toward recruiting Jane through marriage.
Jane must distinguish genuine divine duty from St. John's powerful interpretation of it.
